stem:
Kenyan filmmaker Wanjiru Kamau spent three fishing seasons documenting cooperatives along Lake Victoria. She had initially envisioned an authoritative voice-over, one that would guide viewers through scenes of nets, markets, and quota ______ screening a rough cut for the fishers, however, she abandoned narration entirely, letting their unscripted exchanges carry the film.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice D is correct. Use the Split Test. "She had initially envisioned an authoritative voice-over, one that would guide viewers through scenes of nets, markets, and quota negotiations" is a complete sentence. "After screening a rough cut for the fishers, however, she abandoned narration entirely, letting their unscripted exchanges carry the film" is also a complete sentence. A period correctly separates them. The "however" sits in the middle of the second sentence. It signals contrast but joins nothing, so it can't do the work at the blank. Trust the Split Test, not your ear.

Choice A is incorrect. "Then" is an adverb, not a FANBOYS conjunction. A comma plus "then" still leaves a comma splice between two complete sentences.

Choice B is incorrect. With no punctuation, the two complete sentences run together and form a run-on sentence.

Choice C is incorrect. A comma alone can't join two complete sentences, so this is a comma splice. The comma looks right before the opening phrase "after screening a rough cut," and the later "however" seems to handle the contrast. But neither one fixes the boundary at the blank.

distractor_notes.A: Comma plus fake joiner: treats the adverb "then" as if it could join two complete sentences, so the result is still a comma splice.
distractor_notes.B: No punctuation: the reader misses where the first sentence ends after the long list and appositive, so the result is a run-on.
distractor_notes.C: Comma alone: the student hears a natural pause before "after screening" and assumes the mid-clause "however" supplies the connection. The result is a comma splice.

topic: Documentary filmmaking: dropping narration in a Lake Victoria fishing film

stem:
Jazz pianist Selin Arslan, whose trio recordings are prized for their seemingly spontaneous harmonic turns, insists that she never composes a solo in ______ spend hours each morning cycling a single chord progression through all twelve keys, so that unfamiliar voicings arrive onstage as reflexes rather than decisions.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice B is correct. Use the Split Test. "Jazz pianist Selin Arslan ... insists that she never composes a solo in advance" is a complete sentence. "She does, however, spend hours each morning cycling a single chord progression..." is also a complete sentence. Two complete sentences need a real join at the split point, which comes right after "advance." A semicolon works there. "However" is only an interrupter inside the second sentence, set off by its own commas. It does not join anything.

Choice A is incorrect. It joins two complete sentences with only a comma after "advance," which is a comma splice. The commas around "however" sound smooth but do nothing at the split: trust the Split Test, not your ear.

Choice C is incorrect. "However" is not a joining word. A comma plus "however" between two complete sentences is still a comma splice.

Choice D is incorrect. It runs the two complete sentences together with no punctuation at the split, which is a run-on.

distractor_notes.A: Comma splice. The student hears "however" set off by commas and accepts it, missing that the split point after "advance" has only a comma.
distractor_notes.C: Comma + fake joiner. The student treats "however" like a FANBOYS conjunction that can join two sentences with a comma.
distractor_notes.D: Run-on. There is no punctuation at all between the two complete sentences.

topic: jazz pianist's practice routine

stem:
Aboriginal rangers in northern Australia, reviving an ancestral practice, set small, low-intensity fires early in the dry season, when grasses are still damp. Much of the burns' value emerges months ______ the hottest part of the year, the patchwork of burned ground they leave behind denies fiercer wildfires the continuous fuel needed to spread.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice C is correct. "Much of the burns' value emerges months later" is a complete sentence. "By the hottest part of the year, the patchwork of burned ground they leave behind denies fiercer wildfires the continuous fuel needed to spread" is also a complete sentence: its subject is "patchwork" and its verb is "denies." The second sentence explains the first, because it spells out what that delayed value is. A colon is the right join.

Choice A is incorrect. "By the hottest part of the year" seems to simply extend "months later," but the sentence then reaches a new subject and verb ("the patchwork ... denies"). A comma alone between two complete sentences is a comma splice.

Choice B is incorrect. With no punctuation, the two complete sentences run together, which is a run-on.

Choice D is incorrect. "Then" is not a FANBOYS conjunction. A comma plus "then" between two complete sentences is still a comma splice.

distractor_notes.A: Comma splice. The student reads "later, by the hottest part of the year" as one time phrase and misses that a second subject and verb follow.
distractor_notes.B: Run-on. The student reads "later by the hottest part of the year" as a single phrase and adds no punctuation between the two complete sentences.
distractor_notes.D: Comma + fake joiner. The student treats "then" as if it could join two complete sentences after a comma.

topic: Aboriginal early dry-season burning

stem:
Because the Pacific Plate creeps northwest over a plume of hot mantle rock that stays relatively stationary, the Hawaiian Islands grow older from southeast to ______ among the oldest of the main islands, has had roughly five million years to erode, whereas Hawaiʻi Island, still fed by active vents, continues to add new land.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice A is correct. The opening "Because..." clause is attached to a complete sentence: "the Hawaiian Islands grow older from southeast to northwest." After that comes a second complete sentence: "Kauaʻi ... has had roughly five million years to erode, whereas Hawaiʻi Island ... continues to add new land." Two complete sentences can be separated by a period.

Choice B is incorrect. It joins two complete sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice. The "Because" opener makes the first part feel unfinished, but its main clause is already complete before the blank.

Choice C is incorrect. It runs the two complete sentences together with no punctuation, which is a run-on.

Choice D is incorrect. "Thus" fits the logic, but it is not a FANBOYS conjunction. A comma plus "thus" still produces a comma splice.

distractor_notes.B: Comma splice. The student thinks the "Because" opener makes the whole first part dependent, so a comma seems enough.
distractor_notes.C: Run-on. There is no punctuation between the two complete sentences.
distractor_notes.D: Comma + fake joiner. The cause-effect meaning of "thus" is tempting, but "thus" cannot join two complete sentences after a comma.

topic: Hawaiian hotspot island ages

stem:
Desert tortoises can spend as much as 95 percent of their lives underground. The burrows they excavate, some extending several meters into compacted soil, are seldom occupied by tortoises ______ the animals known to take refuge in these tunnels are burrowing owls, kangaroo rats, and a variety of snakes and lizards.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice A is correct. "The burrows they excavate ... are seldom occupied by tortoises alone" is a complete sentence. "Among the animals known to take refuge in these tunnels are burrowing owls, kangaroo rats, and a variety of snakes and lizards" looks like a phrase, but it is an inverted complete sentence. Its subject is "burrowing owls, kangaroo rats, and a variety of snakes and lizards," and its verb is "are." Flip it to check: "Burrowing owls ... are among the animals...." A semicolon correctly joins the two complete sentences.

Choice B is incorrect. "Alone, among the animals" sounds like a phrase continuing the first sentence, but the second part has its own subject and verb. A comma alone between them is a comma splice.

Choice C is incorrect. It runs the two complete sentences together with no punctuation, which is a run-on.

Choice D is incorrect. "However" is not a joining word. A comma plus "however" between two complete sentences is still a comma splice.

distractor_notes.B: Comma splice. The student reads "among the animals..." as a prepositional phrase tacked onto the first sentence and misses the inverted subject and verb ("are burrowing owls...").
distractor_notes.C: Run-on. The student reads "alone among the animals" as one phrase and adds no punctuation.
distractor_notes.D: Comma + fake joiner. The student treats "however" as if it could join two complete sentences after a comma.

topic: desert tortoise burrows shared by other animals

stem:
Many American libraries of the early nineteenth century were subscription libraries, open only to members who paid annual dues. The library that opened in 1868 in the mill town of Carver Falls, funded by a physician's bequest, admitted readers free of ______ two years, its register listed more than a thousand cardholders.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice B is correct. The word "however" contrasts the Carver Falls library, which charged nothing, with the dues-charging subscription libraries in the first sentence. So "however" belongs at the end of the first clause: the library "admitted readers free of charge, however." Split Test: "The library... admitted readers free of charge, however" is a complete sentence, and "within two years, its register listed more than a thousand cardholders" is another. A semicolon correctly joins them.

Choice A is incorrect. The semicolon is in a legal spot, but it moves "however" into the second clause. That sets the jump in cardholders against free admission. Free admission explains the jump; it does not contrast with it.

Choice C is incorrect. This is a comma splice. "However" is not a joining word, so commas alone cannot connect the two complete sentences.

Choice D is incorrect. This is a run-on. Nothing separates the two complete sentences, and "however" is not set off.

distractor_notes.A: Reflexive "; however," placement: attaches the contrast word to the wrong clause, so it illogically contrasts the jump in cardholders with free admission.
distractor_notes.C: Comma splice with a fake joiner: treats "however" as if it could join two independent clauses with commas.
distractor_notes.D: Run-on: no punctuation between two independent clauses, and "however" is not set off.

topic: Free town library replacing subscription libraries, 1868

stem:
The Hawaiian Islands formed as the Pacific Plate, drifting slowly northwest, passed over a hotspot in Earth's mantle. Successive volcanoes grew above the hotspot, but the plate's steady motion eventually carried them away from the plume that had built ______ off from their magma supply, these aging volcanoes stopped erupting and began to erode.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice A is correct. Split Test: "Successive volcanoes grew above the hotspot, but the plate's steady motion eventually carried them away from the plume that had built them" is a complete sentence. Its ", but" is already a proper join inside it. "Cut off from their magma supply, these aging volcanoes stopped erupting and began to erode" is a second complete sentence. A period correctly separates them. The opening phrase "cut off from their magma supply" describes "these aging volcanoes."

Choice B is incorrect. This is a comma splice. The commas around "cut off from their magma supply" make it look like a harmless inserted phrase describing "them." But "these aging volcanoes stopped" brings in a new subject and verb, so a comma alone cannot join it to the first sentence. Trust the Split Test, not your ear.

Choice C is incorrect. This is a run-on. Nothing separates the two complete sentences.

Choice D is incorrect. "Therefore" is not a FANBOYS conjunction. A comma plus "therefore" is still a comma splice.

distractor_notes.B: Comma splice disguised by inner commas: reads "cut off from their magma supply" as a nonessential phrase describing "them" and misses the new subject "these aging volcanoes."
distractor_notes.C: Run-on: no punctuation at the boundary between two independent clauses.
distractor_notes.D: Comma + fake joiner: treats "therefore" as if it could join two independent clauses the way "and" or "so" can.

topic: Hawaiian hotspot and volcanic island formation

stem:
Elephants use more than loud trumpets to stay in touch. Their low-frequency rumbles, which often include tones too deep for human ears to detect______ can carry for several kilometers, letting separated members of a family group keep track of one another.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation:
Choice D is correct. The clause "which often include tones too deep for human ears to detect" is extra information about the rumbles. It opens with a comma after "rumbles," so it must close with a comma too. Only the monarchs fit that description, so "the monarchs" must come right after the comma. Choice D does this: the monarchs never made the trip, and the monarchs hold a southwesterly heading.
